title: Book 4, Chapter 14 — Eighth and Ninth Years of the War—Invasion of Boeotia—Fall of Amphipolis—Brilliant Successes of Brasidas
paragraphs: The same summer the Mitylenians were about to fortify Antandrus, as they had intended. But Demodocus and Aristides, who commanded the Athenian squadron collecting subsidies, heard on the Hellespont what was being done there (their colleague Lamachus had sailed into the Pontus with ten ships). They feared that the place would become a second Anaia — the town where the Samian exiles had settled to harass Samos, where they helped the Peloponnesians by sending pilots to their navy, and where they kept the city in agitation by receiving all its outlaws. So they gathered a force from the allies and sailed against Antandrus, defeated the troops that came out to meet them, and recovered the place. Not long afterwards Lamachus, who had sailed into the Pontus, lost his ships at anchor in the river Calex, in the territory of Heraclea. Rain had fallen in the interior, and the flood came down suddenly upon them. He and his men then went by land through the Bithynian Thracians on the Asiatic side and reached Chalcedon, the Megarian colony at the mouth of the Pontus.

The same summer the Athenian general Demosthenes arrived at Naupactus with forty ships, immediately after the return from the Megarid. Certain men in the cities of Boeotia, who wished to change their constitution and introduce a democracy like the one at Athens, had made overtures to Hippocrates and to him. Ptoeodorus, a Theban exile, was the chief mover in this intrigue. One party was to betray to them Siphae, the seaport in the bay of Crisae, in Thespian territory. Another party was to put Chaeronea into their hands. (Chaeronea is a dependency of the city once called the Minyan, now the Boeotian, Orchomenus.) The exiles from that town were very active in the business and were hiring men in Peloponnese. Some Phocians were also in the plot, since Chaeronea is the frontier town of Boeotia and lies close to Phanotis in Phocia. Meanwhile the Athenians were to seize Delium, the sanctuary of Apollo in the territory of Tanagra, facing Euboea. All these things were to happen at once, on an appointed day, so that the Boeotians could not unite to oppose them at Delium, being kept busy everywhere by disturbances at home. If the enterprise succeeded and Delium was fortified, its authors confidently expected that things would not stay as they were, even if no revolution followed at once in Boeotia. With these places in their hands, the country harassed by raids, and a refuge always near for the partisans who took part in them, the rebels would be supported by the Athenians and the forces of the oligarchs would be divided. After a while it would then be possible to settle matters as they wished.

Such was the plot in contemplation. Hippocrates, with a force raised at home, waited for the right moment to take the field against the Boeotians. He sent Demosthenes ahead with the forty ships to Naupactus, to raise an army of Acarnanians and other allies in that region and then sail to receive Siphae from the conspirators. A day had been agreed for both operations to take place together. When Demosthenes arrived, he found that the united Acarnanians had already forced Oeniadae to join the Athenian confederacy. He raised all the allies in those countries himself, marched against Salynthius and the Agraeans, and subdued them. After that he turned to the preparations he needed to be at Siphae by the appointed time.

About the same time in the summer, Brasidas set out on his march to the Thracian places with seventeen hundred heavy infantry. Arriving at Heraclea in Trachis, he sent a messenger from there to his friends at Pharsalus, asking them to conduct him and his army through the country. So there came to Melitia in Achaia Panaerus, Dorus, Hippolochidas, Torylaus and Strophacus, the Chalcidian proxenus, and under their escort he resumed his march. Other Thessalians accompanied him as well, among them Niconidas from Larissa, a friend of Perdiccas. It was never very easy to cross Thessaly without an escort, and throughout Hellas it was a delicate step for an armed force to pass without leave through a neighbor’s country. Besides this, the Thessalian people had always sympathized with the Athenians. Indeed, if Thessaly had had a constitutional government instead of its customary close oligarchy, he would never have been able to go on, since even as it was he was met at the river Enipeus by certain men of the opposite party, who forbade him to go further and complained that he was making the attempt without the consent of the nation. His escort answered that they had no intention of taking him through against their will; they were only friends attending an unexpected visitor. Brasidas himself added that he came as a friend to Thessaly and its inhabitants, that his arms were directed not against them but against the Athenians, with whom he was at war, and that although he knew of no quarrel between the Thessalians and the Lacedaemonians to prevent the two nations from having access to each other’s territory, he neither would nor could go on against their wishes; he could only beg them not to stop him. With this answer they went away. He then took the advice of his escort and pushed on without halting, before a greater force could gather to prevent him. So on the very day he set out from Melitia he covered the whole distance to Pharsalus and encamped on the river Apidanus. From there he went on to Phacium, and from Phacium to Perrhaebia. Here his Thessalian escort turned back, and the Perrhaebians, who are subjects of Thessaly, set him down at Dium in the dominions of Perdiccas. Dium is a Macedonian town under Mount Olympus, facing Thessaly.

In this way Brasidas hurried through Thessaly before anyone could get ready to stop him, and reached Perdiccas and Chalcidice. The army had been brought out of Peloponnese by the Thracian towns in revolt against Athens and by Perdiccas, who was alarmed at the Athenian successes. The Chalcidians thought they would be the first target of an Athenian expedition. (Not that the neighboring towns which had not yet revolted were not also secretly party to the invitation.) Perdiccas, for his part, had fears of his own because of his old quarrels with the Athenians, although he was not openly at war with them, and above all he wished to reduce Arrhabaeus, king of the Lyncestians. It had been less difficult for them to get an army to leave Peloponnese because of the Lacedaemonians’ ill fortune at the present moment. The Athenian attacks upon Peloponnese, and in particular upon Laconia, might, it was hoped, be diverted most effectively by annoying the Athenians in return, and by sending an army to their allies, especially as these were willing to maintain it and had asked for it to aid them in revolting. The Lacedaemonians were also glad to have an excuse for sending some of the Helots out of the country, for fear that the present state of affairs and the occupation of Pylos might encourage them to rise. Indeed, fear of the Helots’ numbers and obstinacy even persuaded the Lacedaemonians to the action which I shall now relate; their policy had always been governed by the need to take precautions against them. The Helots were invited by proclamation to pick out those of their number who claimed to have distinguished themselves most against the enemy, so that they might receive their freedom. The aim was to test them, since it was thought that the first to claim their freedom would be the most high-spirited and the most likely to rebel. As many as two thousand were selected in this way. They crowned themselves and went round the temples, rejoicing in their new freedom. The Spartans, however, did away with them soon afterwards, and no one ever knew how each of them perished. So the Spartans now gladly sent seven hundred Helots as heavy infantry with Brasidas, who recruited the rest of his force with money in Peloponnese.

Brasidas himself was sent out by the Lacedaemonians mainly at his own desire, although the Chalcidians were also eager to have him. He had shown himself a thorough man whenever anything had to be done at Sparta, and his later service abroad proved of the utmost use to his country. At the present moment his just and moderate conduct toward the towns generally succeeded in procuring their revolt, besides the places he managed to take by treachery. So when the Lacedaemonians wished to treat, as they ultimately did, they had places to offer in exchange, and meanwhile the burden of war was lifted from Peloponnese. Later in the war, after the events in Sicily, it was the valor and conduct Brasidas showed at this time, known by experience to some and by hearsay to others, that chiefly created among the allies of Athens a feeling for the Lacedaemonians. He was the first to go out and show himself so good a man in every respect that he left behind the conviction that the rest were like him.

Meanwhile the Athenians learned of his arrival in the Thracian country, and no sooner had they heard of it than they declared war against Perdiccas, whom they regarded as the author of the expedition, and kept a closer watch on their allies in that quarter.

Upon the arrival of Brasidas and his army, Perdiccas immediately set out with them and with his own forces against his neighbor Arrhabaeus, son of Bromerus, king of the Lyncestian Macedonians. He had a quarrel with him and wished to subdue him. But when he reached the pass leading into Lyncus with his army and Brasidas, Brasidas told him that before starting hostilities he wished to go and try to persuade Arrhabaeus to become an ally of Lacedaemon. Arrhabaeus had already made overtures, saying he was willing to make Brasidas arbitrator between them. The Chalcidian envoys who accompanied Brasidas had also warned him not to remove the apprehensions of Perdiccas, so as to ensure his greater zeal in their cause. Besides, the envoys of Perdiccas had talked at Lacedaemon about his bringing many of the places around him into alliance with them; and so Brasidas thought he might take a larger view of the question of Arrhabaeus. Perdiccas retorted that he had not brought him along to arbitrate in their quarrel, but to put down the enemies he might point out to him, and that while he, Perdiccas, maintained half the army, it was a breach of faith for Brasidas to parley with Arrhabaeus. Nevertheless Brasidas disregarded the wishes of Perdiccas and held the parley in spite of him, and let himself be persuaded to lead the army away without invading the country of Arrhabaeus. After this Perdiccas, holding that faith had not been kept with him, contributed only a third instead of half of the support of the army.

That same summer Brasidas lost no time. A little before the vintage he marched with the Chalcidians against Acanthus, a colony of the Andrians. The people of the town were split over whether to receive him: on one side were those who had joined the Chalcidians in inviting him, on the other the popular party. Still, fear for their fruit, which was not yet gathered, let Brasidas persuade the multitude to let him in alone and hear him before deciding. He was admitted and came before the people, and, as a speaker not bad for a Lacedaemonian, he addressed them as follows:

“Acanthians, the Lacedaemonians have sent me and my army to make good the reason we gave when we began the war: that we were fighting the Athenians in order to free Hellas. If we have been slow to come, the cause was a mistaken hope about how the war at home would go. We expected to bring the Athenians down quickly by our own efforts alone, with no risk to you, and you must not blame us for that. We have come as soon as we could, and we mean, with your help, to do our best to subdue them. Meanwhile it astonishes me to find your gates closed against me and no better welcome waiting. We Lacedaemonians took you for allies who were eager for us, and thought we would be with you in spirit before we ever arrived in body. That is why we accepted every risk of a march of many days through a strange country: our zeal carried us that far. It would be a terrible thing if you now had other plans, and meant to block your own freedom and that of Hellas. You do more than oppose me yourselves. Wherever I go, people will be less ready to join me, because you, the first to whom I came — a considerable town like Acanthus, and men as prudent as the Acanthians — refused to receive me. I shall then have nothing to prove that the reason I give is the true one. People will say either that the freedom I offer is somehow unfair, or that my force is too weak to protect you if Athens attacks. Yet when I went with this same army to relieve Nisaea, the Athenians had the larger force and still did not dare to engage me. It is unlikely that they will ever send across the sea against you an army as large as the one they had at Nisaea. As for me, I have not come to hurt the Hellenes but to free them. The solemn oaths by which I have bound my government, that every ally I bring over shall be independent, bear witness to it. And I do not come to win your alliance by force or by fraud. I come to offer you mine, to help you against your Athenian masters. After the guarantees I offer, then, I protest against any suspicion of my intentions, and equally against any doubt of my power to protect you; and I invite you to join me without hesitation.

“Some of you may hold back because they have private enemies, and fear that I will hand the city over to a party. None need be more at ease than they. I have not come to help this party or that. I would not call it bringing you freedom in any real sense if I ignored your constitution and enslaved the many to the few or the few to the many. That would be heavier than a foreign yoke, and we Lacedaemonians, instead of earning thanks for our trouble, would win neither honor nor glory, but reproaches instead. The very charges that strengthen our hands in the war against the Athenians would, by our own admission, apply to us, and be more hateful in us than in those who make no claim to honesty. For it is more disgraceful for men of character to seize what they covet by plausible fraud than by open force. Force has at least the justification of the might that fortune gives; the other is plain roguery, however clever. A matter that touches us so closely we naturally guard most jealously. And beyond the oaths I have mentioned, what stronger assurance can you have than this: that when you set our words beside the facts, you are convinced it is in our interest to do as we say?

“Suppose you answer these considerations of mine with a plea of inability, and claim that your friendly feeling should excuse you from harm for refusing. Suppose you say that, in your opinion, freedom is not without its dangers, and that it is right to offer it to those able to accept it but not to force it on anyone unwilling. Then I shall call on the gods and heroes of your country to witness that I came for your good and was turned away, and I shall do my best to compel you by laying waste your land. I shall do so without scruple, justified by the necessity that binds me. First, I must keep the Lacedaemonians from being damaged by you, their friends, if you stay out, through the money you pay to the Athenians. Second, I must keep the Hellenes from being held back by you as they shake off their servitude. Otherwise we would have no right to act as we propose. Apart from some public interest, what call would we Lacedaemonians have to free people who do not wish to be free? Empire is not our aim: we are laboring to put it down. And we would wrong the greater number if we let you stand in the way of the independence we offer to all. So try to decide wisely. Make a start on the liberation of the Hellenes, lay up endless renown for yourselves, spare yourselves private loss, and cover your commonwealth with glory.”

Such were the words of Brasidas. A great deal was said on both sides, and then the Acanthians voted in secret. The majority, swayed by the seductive arguments of Brasidas and by fear for their fruit, decided to revolt from Athens. Even so, they would not admit the army until he had given his personal guarantee for the oaths his government had sworn before sending him out, which assured independence to the allies he might bring over. Not long afterwards Stagirus, a colony of the Andrians, followed their example and revolted.

Such were the events of this summer. In the first days of the following winter, the places in Boeotia were to be handed over to the Athenian generals Hippocrates and Demosthenes: Demosthenes was to go with his ships to Siphae, Hippocrates to Delium. A mistake was made, however, about the days on which each was to start. Demosthenes sailed to Siphae first, with the Acarnanians and many allies from those parts on board, and accomplished nothing, because the plot had been betrayed. Nicomachus, a Phocian from Phanotis, had told the Lacedaemonians, who told the Boeotians. Help therefore poured in from all over Boeotia, since Hippocrates was not yet there to create his diversion. Siphae and Chaeronea were quickly secured, and the conspirators, who learned of the mistake, did not dare to make any move in the towns.

Meanwhile Hippocrates made a levy in mass of the citizens, resident aliens and foreigners at Athens. He reached his destination after the Boeotians had already returned from Siphae. He encamped his army and began to fortify Delium, the sanctuary of Apollo, in this way. They dug a trench all around the temple and the sacred ground, and the earth thrown up from the digging served as a wall, in which stakes were also set. They cut down the vines around the sanctuary and threw them in, along with stones and bricks pulled from the houses nearby; in short, they used every means to raise the rampart quickly. They also built wooden towers wherever they were needed, and at places where no part of the temple buildings remained, as on the side where the gallery that used to stand there had collapsed. They began the work on the third day after leaving home, kept at it through the fourth, and continued until dinnertime on the fifth. By then most of it was finished, and the army set out from Delium and went about a mile and a quarter on its way home. From there most of the light troops went straight on, while the heavy infantry halted and remained where they were. Hippocrates had stayed behind at Delium to arrange the posts and to direct the completion of the parts of the outworks still unfinished.

While the Athenians were thus occupied, the Boeotians were mustering at Tanagra. By the time they had come in from all the towns, the Athenians were already on their way home. The rest of the eleven Boeotarchs were against giving battle, because the enemy was no longer in Boeotia; the Athenians had halted just across the Oropian border. But Pagondas, son of Aeolidas, thought it best to risk a battle. He was one of the two Boeotarchs of Thebes (the other being Arianthides, son of Lysimachidas) and was then in supreme command. He called the men to him company by company, so that they would not all leave their arms at once, and urged them to attack the Athenians and face the issue of a battle. He spoke as follows:

“Boeotians, none of us, your generals, should ever have entertained the idea that we must not give battle to the Athenians unless we catch up with them in Boeotia. They crossed our frontier and built a fort in our country to harm Boeotia. They are therefore, I think, our enemies wherever we meet them, and from whatever place they have come to behave as enemies do. And if anyone has adopted that idea out of concern for safety, it is high time for him to change his mind. Men attacked, with their own country in danger, can hardly weigh what is prudent as calmly as men who enjoy all they possess and are considering an attack on a neighbor in order to gain more. It is your national habit to offer the same resistance to a foreign invader, whether at home or abroad; and when the invader is Athenian and lives right on your frontier, it is doubly necessary. Between neighbors in general, freedom means nothing more than a resolve to hold one’s own. With neighbors like these, who seek to enslave near and far alike, there is nothing for it but to fight to the last. Consider the condition of the Euboeans and of most of the rest of Hellas, and be convinced of this. Others fight their neighbors over this frontier or that. For us, conquest would mean a single frontier for the whole country, about which there could be no dispute, because they would simply come and take by force what we have. We have that much more to fear from this neighbor than from any other. Besides, men who are tempted by pride in their strength to attack their neighbors, as the Athenians are now, usually march with most confidence against those who keep quiet and only defend themselves in their own land. They think twice about grappling with those who meet them outside their frontier and strike the first blow when they get the chance. The Athenians have shown us this themselves. We defeated them at Coronea, when our quarrels had let them occupy the country, and that defeat has kept Boeotia very secure until today. Remembering this, the old men must match their ancient exploits, and the young, the sons of the heroes of that time, must try not to disgrace their native valor. Let us trust in the help of the god whose temple has been fortified in defiance of religion, and in the victims, which our sacrifices have shown to be favorable, and let us march against the enemy. Let us teach him to go and take what he wants by attacking someone who will not resist him; and to learn that men whose glory is to be always ready to fight for the liberty of their own country, and never to enslave another’s unjustly, will not let him leave without a struggle.”

By these arguments Pagondas persuaded the Boeotians to attack the Athenians. It was already late in the day, but he quickly broke camp and led his army forward. Near the enemy, he halted at a spot where a hill stood between the two armies and hid them from each other, and there he drew up his men and prepared for action. Meanwhile Hippocrates at Delium was told that the Boeotians were coming. He ordered his troops to form line and joined them himself shortly afterwards, leaving about three hundred horse at Delium, to guard the place if it were attacked and to wait for a chance to fall on the Boeotians during the battle. The Boeotians stationed a detachment to deal with these. When all was arranged to their satisfaction, they came over the hill and halted in the order they had chosen. They numbered seven thousand heavy infantry, more than ten thousand light troops, one thousand horse and five hundred targeteers. The Thebans and the people of their province held the right. In the center were the Haliartians, Coronaeans, Copaeans and the other peoples around the lake, and on the left the Thespians, Tanagraeans and Orchomenians. Cavalry and light troops stood at the end of each wing. The Thebans were drawn up twenty-five shields deep; the rest chose their own depth. Such was the strength and arrangement of the Boeotian army.

On the Athenian side, the heavy infantry formed eight deep along the whole line, equal in number to the enemy, with the cavalry on the two wings. There were no regularly armed light troops in the army, and there never had been any at Athens. The men who had joined the invasion were many times more numerous than the enemy’s, but most had followed unarmed, as part of the levy in mass of citizens and foreigners from Athens. They had started home first and were not present in any number. The armies were now in line and about to engage. Hippocrates, the general, went along the Athenian ranks and encouraged them as follows:

“Athenians, I shall say only a few words, but brave men need no more, and my words are meant more for your understanding than for your courage. None of you should imagine that we are going out of our way to run this risk in a foreign country. The battle will be fought in their territory, but it will be for ours. If we win, the Peloponnesians will never again invade your country without the Boeotian horse, and in one battle you will gain Boeotia and, in a manner, free Attica. So advance to meet them as citizens of a country in which you all take pride as the first in Hellas, and as sons of the fathers who defeated them at Oenophyta under Myronides and so became masters of Boeotia.”

Hippocrates had gone only halfway through the army with his exhortation when the Boeotians, after a few more hurried words from Pagondas, sang the paean and came down against them from the hill. The Athenians advanced to meet them and closed at a run. The outer wing of neither army took part, since water-courses in the way stopped both. The rest fought with the utmost obstinacy, shield against shield. The Athenians worsted the Boeotian left as far as the center, and the Thespians in that part of the field suffered most. The troops beside them had given way; the Thespians were surrounded in a narrow space and cut down in hand-to-hand fighting. Some of the Athenians too fell into confusion while surrounding the enemy, and mistook their own men for the enemy and killed them. In this part of the field the Boeotians were beaten and fell back on the troops still fighting. On the right, however, where the Thebans were, the Boeotians got the better of the Athenians and pushed them further and further back, though slowly at first. It also happened that Pagondas, seeing his left in distress, had sent two squadrons of horse around the hill, out of sight. When they suddenly appeared, panic struck the victorious Athenian wing, which thought another army was coming against it. At length, in both parts of the field, thrown into panic and with their line broken by the advancing Thebans, the whole Athenian army took to flight. Some made for Delium and the sea, some for Oropus, others for Mount Parnes, or wherever they had hope of safety. The Boeotians pursued and cut them down, and so especially did the cavalry, made up partly of Boeotians and partly of Locrians, who had come up just as the rout began. But night came on and cut short the pursuit, and the mass of the fugitives escaped more easily than they otherwise would have. The next day the troops at Oropus and Delium went home by sea, leaving a garrison in Delium, which they kept holding in spite of the defeat.

The Boeotians set up a trophy, collected their own dead and stripped the enemy’s. Leaving a guard over the bodies, they withdrew to Tanagra to plan their attack on Delium. Meanwhile a herald came from the Athenians to ask for the dead. A Boeotian herald met him and turned him back, telling him that he would achieve nothing until the Boeotian herald himself returned. This man then went on to the Athenians and told them, on behalf of the Boeotians, that they had done wrong in breaking the law of the Hellenes. What was the use of the universal custom that protects the temples in an invaded country, if the Athenians were to fortify Delium and live there, behaving exactly as if they were on unconsecrated ground, and drawing and using for their own purposes the water that the Boeotians themselves never touched except for sacred uses? Therefore, for the sake of the god as well as of themselves, and in the name of the deities concerned and of Apollo, the Boeotians called on them first to leave the temple, if they wished to take up the dead who belonged to them.

When the herald had spoken, the Athenians sent their own herald to the Boeotians with this message. They had done no wrong to the temple, and in future they would do it no more harm than they could avoid. They had not occupied it originally with any such design, but to defend themselves from it against those who were truly wronging them. The law of the Hellenes was that whoever conquered a country, large or small, took possession of its temples along with it, and was bound to keep up the customary ceremonies, at least as far as possible. The Boeotians, and most other peoples who had driven out the owners of a country and put themselves in their place by force, now held as of right the temples that they had first entered as usurpers. If the Athenians had been able to conquer more of Boeotia, the same would be true of them. As things stood, they would treat the part they had taken as their own, and would not leave it unless forced to. As for the water, they had disturbed it under the pressure of a necessity that they had not brought on themselves wantonly, since they had been forced to use it in defending themselves against the Boeotians, who had first invaded Attica. Besides, anything done under the pressure of war and danger might reasonably claim indulgence even in the eyes of the god. Why else were the altars a refuge for involuntary offenses? Transgression, too, was a term applied to presumptuous offenders, not to the victims of adverse circumstances. In short, which were the more impious: the Boeotians, who wished to barter dead bodies for holy places, or the Athenians, who refused to give up holy places in order to obtain what was theirs by right? The condition of evacuating Boeotia must therefore be withdrawn. They were no longer in Boeotia. They stood where they stood by the right of the sword. All that the Boeotians had to do was to tell them to take up their dead under a truce, according to the national custom.

The Boeotians replied that if the Athenians were in Boeotia, they must leave that country before taking up their dead. If they were in their own territory, they could do as they pleased. The Boeotians knew that the Oropid, where the bodies happened to be lying (the battle having been fought on the border), was subject to Athens, but they also knew that the Athenians could not get the bodies without Boeotian leave. Besides, why should they grant a truce for Athenian ground? And what could be fairer than to tell the Athenians to leave Boeotia if they wished to get what they asked for? So the Athenian herald went back with this answer, having failed in his errand.

At once the Boeotians sent for darters and slingers from the Malian Gulf. Joined by two thousand Corinthian heavy infantry who had come to them after the battle, by the Peloponnesian garrison that had left Nisaea, and by some Megarians, they marched against Delium and attacked the fort. After various efforts they finally took it, with an engine of the following kind. They sawed a great beam in two, hollowed it out from end to end and fitted it neatly together again like a pipe. At one end they hung a cauldron by chains, with an iron tube projecting from the beam into it, and they plated much of the beam itself with iron. They brought this up on carts from a distance to the part of the wall made mostly of vines and timber. When it was near, they inserted huge bellows into their end of the beam and blew. The blast, tightly confined, passed into the cauldron, which was filled with lighted coals, sulphur and pitch. It made a great blaze and set fire to the wall, which soon became impossible to hold. The defenders left it and fled, and in this way the fort was taken. Of the garrison, some were killed and two hundred were made prisoners. Most of the rest got on board their ships and went home.

Delium fell seventeen days after the battle. Soon afterward the Athenian herald, who did not know what had happened, came again for the dead. The Boeotians now gave them back, and no longer answered as they had at first. Not quite five hundred Boeotians fell in the battle, and nearly one thousand Athenians, including Hippocrates the general, besides a great number of light troops and camp followers.

Soon after this battle, Demosthenes made a landing on the Sicyonian coast, after the failure of his voyage to Siphae and of the plot on the town. He used the Acarnanian and Agraean troops and the four hundred Athenian heavy infantry that he had on board. But before all his ships had reached the shore, the Sicyonians came up, routed those who had landed and chased them to their ships, killing some and taking others prisoner. They then set up a trophy and gave back the dead under a truce.

At about the same time as the affair at Delium, Sitalces, king of the Odrysians, died. He was defeated in battle during a campaign against the Triballi. His nephew Seuthes, son of Sparadocus, succeeded him as king of the Odrysians and of the rest of the Thracian territory that Sitalces had ruled.

The same winter Brasidas marched with his allies from the Thracian places against Amphipolis, the Athenian colony on the river Strymon. Aristagoras of Miletus (when he fled from King Darius) had earlier tried to settle the spot where the city now stands, but the Edonians drove him out. Thirty-two years later the Athenians tried, sending ten thousand settlers of their own citizens and anyone else who chose to go; these were cut off at Drabescus by the Thracians. Twenty-nine years after that, the Athenians returned, with Hagnon, son of Nicias, sent out as leader of the colony. They drove out the Edonians and founded a town on the spot, formerly called Ennea Hodoi or Nine Ways. They set out from Eion, their commercial seaport at the mouth of the river, not more than three miles from the present town. Hagnon named the town Amphipolis because the Strymon flows round it on two sides. He built it so that it could be seen from sea and land alike, and ran a long wall across from river to river to complete the circuit.

Brasidas now marched against this town, starting from Arne in Chalcidice. He reached Aulon and Bromiscus, where the lake of Bolbe runs into the sea, at about dusk. There he ate his supper and went on during the night. The weather was stormy and it was snowing a little, which encouraged him to hurry. He hoped, if possible, to take everyone in Amphipolis by surprise, except the party who were to betray it. The plot was run by some natives of Argilus, an Andrian colony, who lived in Amphipolis, where they also had other accomplices won over by Perdiccas or the Chalcidians. But the most active were the inhabitants of Argilus itself, which is close by. The Athenians had always suspected them, and they had always had designs on the place. Now they saw their opportunity arrive with Brasidas. They had for some time been in correspondence with their countrymen in Amphipolis about betraying the town. They at once received him into Argilus and revolted from the Athenians, and that same night took him on to the bridge over the river. There he found only a small guard to oppose him, since the town lay some distance from the crossing and the walls did not reach down to it as they do now. He easily drove this guard in, partly because there was treason in their ranks, and partly because of the stormy weather and the suddenness of his attack. So he got across the bridge and immediately became master of all the property outside, the Amphipolitans having houses all over that quarter.

The crossing of Brasidas was a complete surprise to the people in the town. Many of those outside were captured and the rest fled within the wall, and together this produced great confusion among the citizens, especially since they did not trust one another. It is even said that if Brasidas, instead of stopping to plunder, had advanced straight against the town, he would probably have taken it. In fact, however, he established himself where he was and overran the country outside. For the present he remained inactive, vainly waiting for a move from his friends within. Meanwhile the party opposed to the traitors was numerous enough to prevent the gates from being opened at once. In concert with Eucles, the general who had come from Athens to defend the place, they sent to the other commander in Thrace, Thucydides, son of Olorus, the author of this history. He was at the isle of Thasos, a Parian colony, half a day’s sail from Amphipolis, and they told him to come to their relief. When he received the message he at once set sail with the seven ships he had with him. He hoped, if possible, to reach Amphipolis in time to prevent its capitulation, or in any case to save Eion.

Meanwhile Brasidas feared that help would arrive by sea from Thasos. He also learned that Thucydides had the right of working the gold mines in that part of Thrace and so had great influence with the people of the mainland. He therefore hurried to gain the town, if he could, before the people of Amphipolis were encouraged by Thucydides’ arrival to hope that he could save them by collecting a force of allies from the sea and from Thrace, and so refuse to surrender. He accordingly offered moderate terms. He proclaimed that any of the Amphipolitans and Athenians who chose could continue to enjoy their property with full rights of citizenship, while those who did not wish to stay had five days to leave, taking their property with them.

When the bulk of the inhabitants heard this, they began to change their minds. Only a small number of the citizens were Athenians, the majority having come from various places, and many of the prisoners outside had relatives within the walls. They found the proclamation a fair one compared with what their fear had led them to expect. The Athenians were glad to leave, since they thought they ran more risk than the rest and did not expect any quick relief. The multitude generally was content to be left in possession of its civic rights, and with such an unexpected escape from danger. The partisans of Brasidas now openly advocated this course, seeing that the feeling of the people had changed and that they no longer listened to the Athenian general who was present. So the surrender was made, and they admitted Brasidas on the terms of his proclamation. In this way they gave up the city, and late the same day Thucydides and his ships entered the harbor of Eion. Brasidas had just gained Amphipolis and had been within a night of taking Eion: if the ships had been less prompt in relieving it, it would have been his by morning.

After this Thucydides put everything in order at Eion to secure it against any present or future attack by Brasidas, and received those who had chosen to come there from the interior, according to the terms agreed. Meanwhile Brasidas suddenly sailed down the river to Eion with a number of boats, to see if he could seize the point running out from the wall and so command the entrance. At the same time he attempted it by land, but he was beaten off on both sides and had to content himself with arranging matters at Amphipolis and in the neighborhood. Myrcinus, an Edonian town, also came over to him, the Edonian king Pittacus having been killed by the sons of Goaxis and by his own wife Brauro. Not long after, Galepsus and Oesime, which are Thasian colonies, followed its example. Perdiccas too came up immediately after the capture and joined in these arrangements.

The news that Amphipolis was in the hands of the enemy caused great alarm at Athens. The town was valuable not only for the timber it supplied for shipbuilding and for the money it brought in. There was also this: the escort of the Thessalians gave the Lacedaemonians a way of reaching the allies of Athens as far as the Strymon, but as long as they were not masters of the bridge, were watched on the side of Eion by the Athenian galleys, and were blocked on the land side by a large and extensive lake formed by the waters of the river, it was impossible for them to go any further. Now, on the contrary, the path seemed open. There was also the fear that the allies would revolt, because of the moderation Brasidas showed in all his conduct, and because of his declarations everywhere that he had been sent out to free Hellas. The towns subject to the Athenians heard of the capture of Amphipolis, of the terms it had been given, and of the gentleness of Brasidas. They felt most strongly encouraged to change their condition, and sent secret messages to him begging him to come to them, each wishing to be the first to revolt. Indeed there seemed to be no danger in doing so. Their mistake in estimating the Athenian power was as great as that power afterwards turned out to be, and their judgment rested more upon blind wishing than upon any sound foresight. For it is a habit of mankind to entrust to careless hope what they long for, and to use sovereign reason to thrust aside what they do not fancy. Besides, the severe blow the Athenians had lately suffered in Boeotia, together with the seductive though untrue statements of Brasidas, that the Athenians had not dared to engage his single army at Nisaea, made the allies confident, and led them to believe that no Athenian force would be sent against them. Above all, the wish to do what was agreeable at the moment, and the likelihood that they would find the Lacedaemonians full of zeal at the start, made them eager to venture. The Athenians saw this and sent garrisons to the different towns, as far as was possible at such short notice and in winter. Brasidas, for his part, sent dispatches to Lacedaemon asking for reinforcements, and himself made preparations to build galleys on the Strymon. The Lacedaemonians, however, did not send him any, partly through envy on the part of their leading men, and partly because they were more intent on recovering the prisoners from the island and ending the war.

The same winter the Megarians took the long walls that the Athenians had occupied and razed them to the foundations. After the capture of Amphipolis, Brasidas marched with his allies against Acte. This is a promontory that runs out from the King’s dike with an inward curve and ends in Athos, a lofty mountain looking toward the Aegean Sea. It contains several towns: Sane, an Andrian colony, close to the canal and facing the sea in the direction of Euboea, and the others, Thyssus, Cleone, Acrothoi, Olophyxus and Dium. These are inhabited by mixed barbarian races speaking the two languages. There is also a small Chalcidian element, but the greater number are Tyrrheno-Pelasgians who once settled in Lemnos and Athens, and Bisaltians, Crestonians and Edonians. The towns are all small ones. Most of them came over to Brasidas, but Sane and Dium held out and saw their land ravaged by him and his army.

When they would not submit, he at once marched against Torone in Chalcidice, which was held by an Athenian garrison. A few persons who were prepared to hand over the town had invited him. He arrived in the dark a little before daybreak and sat down with his army near the temple of the Dioscuri, rather more than a quarter of a mile from the city. The rest of the town of Torone and the Athenians in the garrison did not notice his approach. But his partisans knew that he was coming (a few of them had secretly gone out to meet him) and were watching for his arrival. As soon as they were aware of it, they took in with them seven light-armed men with daggers, under the command of Lysistratus, an Olynthian. These seven alone, of twenty men ordered on this service, dared to enter. They passed through the sea wall and, without being seen, went up and put to the sword the garrison of the highest post in the town, which stands on a hill. Then they broke open the postern on the side of Canastraeum.

Brasidas meanwhile came a little nearer and then halted with his main body. He sent on one hundred targeteers to be ready to rush in first, the moment a gate should be thrown open and the beacon lighted as agreed. After some time had passed in waiting and wondering at the delay, the targeteers gradually got up close to the town. The Toronaeans inside, who were at work with the party that had entered, had by this time broken down the postern. They had also opened the gates leading to the market-place by cutting through the bar. First they brought some men round and let them in by the postern, in order to strike panic into the surprised townsmen by attacking them suddenly from behind and on both sides at once. After that they raised the fire-signal as agreed and took in the rest of the targeteers by the market gates.

When Brasidas saw the signal, he told the troops to rise and dashed forward amid the loud shouts of his men, which carried dismay among the astonished townspeople. Some burst in straight through the gate, others climbed over some squared timbers placed against the wall (which had fallen down and was being rebuilt) to draw up stones. Brasidas and the greater number made straight uphill for the higher part of the town, in order to take it from top to bottom and settle the matter once for all, while the rest of the multitude spread in all directions.

The town was captured before the great body of the Toronaeans had recovered from their surprise and confusion. But the conspirators and the citizens of their party at once joined the invaders. About fifty of the Athenian heavy infantry happened to be sleeping in the market-place when the alarm reached them. A few of these were killed fighting, and the rest escaped, some by land, others to the two ships on the station. They took refuge in Lecythus, a fort garrisoned by their own men in the corner of the town that runs out into the sea and is cut off by a narrow isthmus. The Toronaeans of their party joined them there.

Day now came, and the town was secure. Brasidas made a proclamation to the Toronaeans who had taken refuge with the Athenians, inviting as many as chose to come out to their homes without fearing for their rights or persons. He also sent a herald to invite the Athenians to accept a truce and to evacuate Lecythus with their property, as being Chalcidian ground. The Athenians refused this offer but asked for a truce for a day to take up their dead. Brasidas granted it for two days, and he used them to fortify the nearby houses, while the Athenians did the same to their positions. Meanwhile he called a meeting of the Toronaeans and said very much what he had said at Acanthus. They must not look upon those who had negotiated with him for the capture of the town as bad men or as traitors, since these had not acted as they had from corrupt motives or in order to enslave the city, but for the good and freedom of Torone. Nor must those who had not shared in the enterprise imagine that they would not equally reap its fruits, since he had not come to destroy either city or individual. This was the reason for his proclamation to those who had fled for refuge to the Athenians. He thought none the worse of them for their friendship for the Athenians. He believed that they had only to make trial of the Lacedaemonians to like them as well, or even much better, since the Lacedaemonians acted much more justly: it was for want of such a trial that they were now afraid of them. Meanwhile he warned all of them to prepare to be staunch allies and to be held responsible for all faults in future. For the past, they had not wronged the Lacedaemonians but had been wronged by others who were too strong for them, and any opposition they might have offered him could be excused.

Having encouraged them with this address, he attacked Lecythus as soon as the truce expired. The Athenians defended themselves from a poor wall and from some houses with parapets. They beat him off one day. The next day the enemy were preparing to bring up an engine from which they meant to throw fire upon the wooden defenses, and the troops were already coming up to the point where they thought they could best bring up the engine and where the place was most open to attack. Meanwhile the Athenians put a wooden tower on a house opposite and carried up a quantity of jars and casks of water and big stones, and a large number of men also climbed up. The house, loaded too heavily, suddenly broke down with a loud crash. The men who were near and saw it were more vexed than frightened. But those who were not so near, and still more those who were furthest off, thought that the place was already taken at that point, and fled in haste to the sea and the ships.

Brasidas saw that they were deserting the parapet, and saw what was going on. He dashed forward with his troops, immediately took the fort and put to the sword all whom he found in it. In this way the Athenians evacuated the place, crossing in their boats and ships to Pallene. Now there is a temple of Athene in Lecythus, and Brasidas, at the moment of making the assault, had proclaimed that he would give thirty silver minae to the first man on the wall. Considering now that the capture was hardly due to human means, he gave the thirty minae to the goddess for her temple. He razed and cleared Lecythus and made the whole of it consecrated ground. He spent the rest of the winter settling the places in his hands and making plans against the rest. With the end of the winter the eighth year of this war ended.

In the spring of the summer following, the Lacedaemonians and Athenians made an armistice for a year. The Athenians thought that they would thus have full leisure to take their precautions before Brasidas could bring about the revolt of any more of their towns, and might also, if it suited them, conclude a general peace. The Lacedaemonians guessed the Athenians’ real fears, and thought that once they had tasted a respite from trouble and misery they would be more disposed to agree to a reconciliation, to give back the prisoners and to make a treaty for a longer period. The great aim of the Lacedaemonians was to get back their men while the good fortune of Brasidas lasted. Further successes might make the struggle in Chalcidice less unequal, but would leave them still deprived of their men, and even in Chalcidice not more than a match for the Athenians and by no means certain of victory. An armistice was accordingly concluded by Lacedaemon and her allies on the following terms:

1. As to the temple and oracle of the Pythian Apollo, we agree that whoever wishes shall have access to it, without fraud or fear, according to the usages of his forefathers. The Lacedaemonians and the allies present agree to this, and promise to send heralds to the Boeotians and Phocians and to do their best to persuade them to agree likewise.

2. As to the treasure of the god, we agree to exert ourselves to detect all those who misappropriate it, truly and honestly following the customs of our forefathers, we and you and all others who are willing, all following the customs of our forefathers. On these points the Lacedaemonians and the other allies are agreed as has been said.

3. As to what follows, the Lacedaemonians and the other allies agree, if the Athenians conclude a treaty, to remain, each of us in our own territory, keeping our respective acquisitions. The garrison in Coryphasium is to keep within Buphras and Tomeus. The garrison in Cythera is not to attempt any communication with the Peloponnesian confederacy, neither we with them, nor they with us. The garrison in Nisaea and Minoa is not to cross the road leading from the gates of the temple of Nisus to that of Poseidon, and from there straight to the bridge at Minoa. The Megarians and the allies are equally bound not to cross this road. The Athenians are to keep the island they have taken, without any communication on either side. As to Troezen, each side is to keep what it has, as was arranged with the Athenians.

4. As to the use of the sea, so far as it concerns their own coast and that of their confederacy, the Lacedaemonians and their allies may voyage upon it in any vessel rowed by oars and of not more than five hundred talents tonnage, but not in a vessel of war.

5. All heralds and embassies, with as many attendants as they please, shall have free passage, going and coming, to Peloponnese or Athens by land and by sea, for concluding the war and adjusting claims.
6. During the truce, deserters, whether slave or free, shall be received neither by you nor by us.
7. Further, satisfaction shall be given by you to us and by us to you according to the public law of our several countries, all disputes being settled by law without recourse to hostilities.

The Lacedaemonians and allies agree to these articles. But if you have anything fairer or juster to suggest, come to Lacedaemon and let us know: whatever is just will meet with no objection from the Lacedaemonians or from the allies. Only let those who come come with full powers, as you require of us. The truce shall be for one year.
Approved by the people.

The tribe of Acamantis had the prytany, Phoenippus was secretary, and Niciades was chairman. Laches moved, in the name of the good luck of the Athenians, that they should conclude the armistice on the terms agreed by the Lacedaemonians and the allies. It was agreed accordingly in the popular assembly that the armistice should be for one year, beginning that very day, the fourteenth of the month of Elaphebolion. During this time ambassadors and heralds should go and come between the two countries to discuss the bases of a pacification. The generals and prytanes should call an assembly of the people, in which the Athenians should first consult on the peace and on the manner in which the embassy for putting an end to the war should be admitted. The embassy now present should at once pledge itself before the people to keep this truce well and truly for one year.

On these terms the Lacedaemonians concluded the armistice with the Athenians and their allies, on the twelfth day of the Spartan month Gerastius, and the allies also took the oaths. Those who concluded it and poured the libation were Taurus, son of Echetimides, Athenaeus, son of Pericleidas, and Philocharidas, son of Eryxidaidas, Lacedaemonians; Aeneas, son of Ocytus, and Euphamidas, son of Aristonymus, Corinthians; Damotimus, son of Naucrates, and Onasimus, son of Megacles, Sicyonians; Nicasus, son of Cecalus, and Menecrates, son of Amphidorus, Megarians; and Amphias, son of Eupaidas, an Epidaurian; and the Athenian generals Nicostratus, son of Diitrephes, Nicias, son of Niceratus, and Autocles, son of Tolmaeus. Such was the armistice, and during the whole of it conferences went on on the subject of a pacification.

While these conferences were going back and forth, Scione, a town in Pallene, revolted from Athens and went over to Brasidas. The Scionaeans say that they are Pallenians from Peloponnese, and that their first settlers, on the voyage home from Troy, were driven to this spot by the storm that caught the Achaeans, and settled there. No sooner had the Scionaeans revolted than Brasidas crossed over to Scione by night. A friendly galley went ahead of him, and he followed some distance behind in a small boat. His thinking was this: if he met a vessel larger than the boat, the galley would defend him; and if a ship that was a match for the galley appeared, it would probably ignore the small vessel and attack the large one, which would give him time to escape. Once across, he called a meeting of the Scionaeans and spoke to the same effect as at Acanthus and Torone. He added that they deserved the highest praise. Pallene within the isthmus was cut off by the Athenian occupation of Potidæa, and their own position was practically that of an island, yet of their own free will they had gone out to meet their liberty. They had not waited timidly until force compelled them to accept what was so plainly for their own good. This was a sign that they would bravely endure any trial, however great. And if he should settle affairs as he intended, he would count them among the truest and sincerest friends of the Lacedaemonians, and would honor them in every other way.

The Scionaeans were elated by his words. Even those who had at first disapproved of what was being done caught the general confidence, and they resolved to carry on the war vigorously. They welcomed Brasidas with every possible honor, publicly crowning him with a crown of gold as the liberator of Hellas, while private persons crowded around him and decked him with garlands as though he were an athlete. For the present Brasidas left them a small garrison and crossed back. Not long afterward he sent over a larger force, intending to attempt Mende and Potidæa with the help of the Scionaeans before the Athenians could arrive. He felt that Scione, being so like an island, would certainly be relieved by them. He also had intelligence in those towns about their betrayal.

While he was engaged in these designs upon the towns, a galley arrived with the commissioners who were carrying round the news of the armistice: Aristonymus for the Athenians and Athenaeus for the Lacedaemonians. The troops crossed back to Torone, and the commissioners gave Brasidas notice of the convention. All the Lacedaemonian allies in Thrace accepted what had been done. Aristonymus raised no difficulty about the rest, but when he counted the days he found that the Scionaeans had revolted after the date of the convention, and he refused to include them. Brasidas objected strongly, asserting that the revolt had taken place before it, and he would not give up the town. When Aristonymus reported the case to Athens, the people at once prepared to send an expedition to Scione. Envoys then arrived from Lacedaemon, who alleged that this would be a breach of the truce, laid claim to the town on the strength of Brasidas’s assertion, and meanwhile offered to submit the question to arbitration. But the Athenians did not choose to risk arbitration. They were determined to send troops to the place at once, and were furious that even islanders now dared to revolt, relying in vain on the power of the Lacedaemonians by land. Besides, the facts of the revolt were rather as the Athenians contended, since the Scionaeans had revolted two days after the convention. Cleon therefore carried a decree to reduce Scione and put the Scionaeans to death, and the Athenians spent the leisure they now enjoyed preparing for the expedition.

Meanwhile Mende revolted. It was a town in Pallene and a colony of the Eretrians. Brasidas received it without scruple, although it had evidently come over during the armistice, because he alleged certain infringements of the truce against the Athenians. Mende was emboldened partly by seeing how forward Brasidas was in the matter, and partly by drawing conclusions from his refusal to betray Scione. Besides, the conspirators in Mende were few, and, as I have already intimated, they had carried on their practices too long not to fear detection for themselves, and not to wish to force the inclination of the multitude. This news made the Athenians more furious than ever, and they at once prepared against both towns. Expecting them to arrive, Brasidas conveyed the women and children of the Scionaeans and Mendaeans away to Olynthus in Chalcidice, and sent over to the two towns five hundred Peloponnesian heavy infantry and three hundred Chalcidian targeteers, all under the command of Polydamidas.

Leaving the two towns to prepare together for the speedy arrival of the Athenians, Brasidas and Perdiccas started on a second joint expedition into Lyncus against Arrhabaeus. Perdiccas brought the forces of his Macedonian subjects and a corps of heavy infantry made up of Hellenes living in the country. Brasidas brought the Peloponnesians he still had with him, and the Chalcidians, Acanthians and the rest, in such force as they were able. In all there were about three thousand Hellenic heavy infantry, accompanied by all the Macedonian cavalry together with the Chalcidians, nearly one thousand strong, besides an immense crowd of barbarians. On entering the country of Arrhabaeus they found the Lyncestians encamped and waiting for them, and took up a position opposite. The infantry on each side were on a hill, with a plain between them. The horse of both armies galloped down into this plain first and fought a cavalry action. After this the Lyncestian heavy infantry advanced from their hill to join their cavalry and offered battle. Brasidas and Perdiccas then also came down to meet them, engaged them and routed them with heavy loss, and the survivors took refuge on the heights and remained there, inactive. The victors set up a trophy and waited two or three days for the Illyrian mercenaries who were to join Perdiccas. Perdiccas then wished to go on and attack the villages of Arrhabaeus, and not to sit still any longer. But Brasidas was afraid that the Athenians might sail up during his absence and that something might happen to Mende, and he saw besides that the Illyrians did not appear. Far from seconding this wish, he was anxious to return.

While they were still disputing, word came that the Illyrians had in fact betrayed Perdiccas and gone over to Arrhabaeus. Because of their warlike reputation, both leaders now thought it best to retreat. But the dispute had left it unsettled when they should start. Night came on, and the Macedonians and the barbarian crowd suddenly took fright, in one of those mysterious panics that great armies are liable to. Convinced that an army many times larger than the one that had really come was upon them, or all but upon them, they broke and ran for home. Perdiccas at first did not see what had happened, and was forced to leave without meeting Brasidas, since the two armies lay encamped far apart. At daybreak Brasidas saw that the Macedonians had gone on, and that the Illyrians and Arrhabaeus were about to attack him. He drew up his heavy infantry in a square with the light troops in the middle, and prepared to retreat as well. He stationed his youngest soldiers to dash out wherever the enemy attacked them. He himself, with three hundred picked men, took the rear, planning to turn about during the retreat and beat off the boldest of their pursuers. Before the enemy came near, he tried to keep up his soldiers’ courage with the following hasty exhortation:

“Peloponnesians, if I did not suspect that you are dismayed at being left alone to face the attack of a numerous barbarian enemy, I would simply say a few words to you as usual, without further explanation. As matters stand, with our friends gone and the enemy so many, I have some advice and information to give you. It must be brief, but I hope it will cover the more important points. The bravery you habitually show in war does not depend on having allies beside you in this or that encounter. It comes from your own native courage. Numbers have no terrors for citizens of states like yours, where the many do not rule the few, but the few rule the many, holding their position by nothing other than superiority in the field. Inexperience now makes you afraid of barbarians. Yet you have already tried your strength against the Macedonians among them, and my own judgment, confirmed by what I hear from others, should be enough to convince you that they will not prove formidable. When an enemy seems strong but is really weak, knowing the facts makes his adversary bolder, just as men who do not know a serious antagonist meet him with the most confidence. The present enemy might terrify an inexperienced imagination. They are formidable in outward bulk, their loud yelling is unbearable, and their weapons, brandished in the air, look threatening. But when it comes to real fighting against an opponent who stands his ground, they are not what they seemed. They keep no regular order, and so feel no shame at abandoning a position when hard pressed. With them flight and attack are equally honorable and prove nothing about courage, and their independent way of fighting always leaves a man who wants to run away with a fair excuse. In short, they think that frightening you from a safe distance is a surer game than meeting you hand to hand; otherwise they would have done the one and not the other. You can plainly see, then, that the terrors that first surrounded them are in fact trifling, though very prominent to eye and ear. Stand your ground when they advance, and again wait for your chance to retire in good order, and you will reach safety all the sooner. You will also know forever afterward that a rabble such as this only shows off its courage, at a distance, by threatening the terrible things it will do to those who withstand its first attack; but against those who give way to it, it is quick enough to show its heroism in pursuit, so long as there is no danger.”

After this brief address Brasidas began to lead his army away. When they saw it, the barbarians came on with loud shouting and uproar, thinking that he was running away and that they would catch him and cut him off. But wherever they charged, they met the young men ready to dash out against them, while Brasidas and his picked company bore the brunt of their onset. The Peloponnesians thus held out against the first attack, to the enemy’s surprise, and then received and drove back each wave as it came, retiring whenever their opponents grew quiet. The main body of the barbarians therefore stopped harassing Brasidas and his Hellenes in the open country. They left a certain number behind to trouble the march, and the rest followed after the fleeing Macedonians, killing all they overtook. They reached in time the narrow pass between two hills that leads into Arrhabaeus’s country. They knew this was the only road by which Brasidas could retreat, and they now moved to surround him as he entered the most impassable part of it, so as to cut him off.

Brasidas saw what they intended. He told his three hundred to run ahead without keeping order, each as fast as he could, to the hill that looked easiest to take, and to try to dislodge the barbarians already there before the main body closed around him and joined them. They attacked and overpowered the party on the hill, and the main army of the Hellenes then moved up toward it with less difficulty. The barbarians were terrified when they saw their men on that side driven off the height and no longer following the main body, who, they supposed, had reached the frontier and got clean away. With the heights secured, Brasidas went on more safely, and that same day reached Arnisa, the first town in the dominions of Perdiccas. The soldiers were enraged at the Macedonians’ desertion. They took out their rage on every yoke of oxen they found on the road, and on any baggage that had fallen off (as could easily happen in the panic of a night retreat): they unyoked the cattle, cut them down, and kept the baggage for themselves. From this moment Perdiccas began to regard Brasidas as an enemy, and to feel toward the Peloponnesians a hatred that did not suit an adversary of the Athenians. Yet he abandoned his natural interests and set himself to make terms with the Athenians and to be rid of the Peloponnesians.

Brasidas came back from Macedonia to Torone and found that the Athenians already held Mende. He stayed quietly where he was, thinking it was now beyond his power to cross into Pallene and help the Mendaeans, but he kept a close watch on Torone. At about the time of the Lyncus campaign, the Athenians had set sail on the expedition that we left them preparing against Mende and Scione. Their force was fifty ships (ten of them Chian), one thousand Athenian heavy infantry, six hundred archers, one hundred Thracian mercenaries, and some targeteers supplied by their allies in the area. Nicias, son of Niceratus, and Nicostratus, son of Diitrephes, commanded. The fleet left Potidæa, landed opposite the temple of Poseidon, and advanced on Mende. The Mendaeans had been reinforced by three hundred Scionaeans and their Peloponnesian auxiliaries, seven hundred heavy infantry in all under Polydamidas. The Athenians found them encamped on a strong hill outside the city. Nicias took one hundred and twenty light-armed Methonaeans, sixty picked Athenian heavy infantry and all the archers, and tried to reach them by a path up the hill. He was wounded and could not force the position. Nicostratus meanwhile led all the rest of the army up the hill, which was naturally difficult, by another approach farther off. His men fell into utter disorder, and the whole Athenian army narrowly escaped defeat. Since the Mendaeans and their allies showed no sign of yielding, the Athenians retreated that day and encamped, and at nightfall the Mendaeans went back into the town.

On the next day the Athenians sailed around to the side facing Scione, took the suburb, and spent the whole day plundering the country. No one came out against them, partly because of unrest inside the town. That night the three hundred Scionaeans went home. The following day Nicias advanced with half the army to the frontier of Scione and laid waste the country, while Nicostratus sat down with the rest before the town, near the upper gate on the road to Potidæa. It happened that the arms of the Mendaeans and their Peloponnesian auxiliaries were piled inside the wall in that quarter, and Polydamidas began to draw them up there for battle, urging the Mendaeans to make a sortie. At that moment one of the popular party answered him in a factious tone that they would not go out and did not want a war. For this answer Polydamidas seized him by the arm and knocked him about. The infuriated commons at once grabbed their arms and rushed upon the Peloponnesians and on their allies of the opposite faction. The men attacked were routed immediately, partly because the clash was so sudden and partly from fear that the gates would be opened to the Athenians, with whom they imagined the attack had been arranged. All who were not killed on the spot fled to the citadel, which they had held from the start. By this time Nicias had returned and was near the city, and the whole Athenian army burst into Mende, whose gates had been opened without any convention. They sacked it as if they had taken it by storm, and the generals had some difficulty even in keeping them from massacring the inhabitants as well. After this the Athenians told the Mendaeans that they could keep their civil rights and judge for themselves those they thought the authors of the revolt. They cut off the party in the citadel with a wall running down to the sea on either side, and set troops to maintain the blockade. Mende thus secured, they moved against Scione.

The Scionaeans and Peloponnesians marched out to meet them. They occupied a strong hill in front of the town, which the enemy had to capture before they could invest the place. The Athenians stormed the hill, defeated its defenders and drove them off, then encamped, set up a trophy, and got ready for the work of circumvallation. Soon after they began, the auxiliaries who had been besieged in the citadel of Mende forced the guard on the seaward side and reached Scione by night. Most of them managed to get into the town, passing through the besieging army.

While the investment of Scione was going on, Perdiccas sent a herald to the Athenian generals and made peace with the Athenians, out of spite against Brasidas for the retreat from Lyncus; he had in fact begun to negotiate from that time. The Lacedaemonian Ischagoras was at that moment about to set out overland with an army to join Brasidas. Nicias now demanded that Perdiccas give the Athenians some proof that his reconciliation was sincere, and Perdiccas himself no longer wanted the Peloponnesians in his country. He therefore stirred up his friends in Thessaly, whose leading men he always took care to keep in touch with, and so thoroughly blocked the army and its preparations that they did not even try the Thessalians. Ischagoras himself, however, with Ameinias and Aristeus, did succeed in reaching Brasidas. The Lacedaemonians had sent them to inspect the situation, and they brought out from Sparta (in violation of all precedent) some of their young men to command the towns, so that the towns would not be entrusted to men on the spot. Brasidas accordingly put Clearidas, son of Cleonymus, in charge of Amphipolis, and Pasitelidas, son of Hegesander, in charge of Torone.

The same summer the Thebans pulled down the wall of the Thespians, on a charge of Atticism. They had always wanted to do it, and found it easy now that the flower of the Thespian youth had been lost in the battle with the Athenians. The same summer the temple of Hera at Argos also burnt down. Chrysis, the priestess, had put a lighted torch near the garlands and then fallen asleep, so that they all caught fire and were in flames before she noticed. Fearing the Argives, Chrysis fled that very night to Phlius. The Argives, as the law provides in such a case, appointed another priestess, named Phaeinis. When Chrysis fled, she had been priestess for eight years of the present war and half of the ninth. At the end of the summer the investment of Scione was complete, and the Athenians left a detachment to maintain the blockade and returned with the rest of their army.

In the following winter the armistice kept the Athenians and Lacedaemonians quiet. But the Mantineans and Tegeans, with their respective allies, fought a battle at Laodicium, in the Oresthid. The victory was left in doubt, for each side routed one of the wings facing it, and both set up trophies and sent spoils to Delphi. Both sides suffered heavy loss, and night broke off the action with the battle undecided. The Tegeans, however, spent the night on the field and set up their trophy at once, whereas the Mantineans withdrew to Bucolion and set up theirs later.

At the end of the same winter, almost in spring, Brasidas made an attempt on Potidæa. He came by night and managed to set a ladder against the wall without being seen, choosing the moment between the passing of the bell from hand to hand and the return of the man who carried it back. But the garrison raised the alarm right afterward, before his men had come up, and he promptly led his troops away without waiting for daylight. So the winter ended, and with it the ninth year of this war of which Thucydides is the historian.
